extracted.intended_audience: firearms dealers, prospective federal firearms licensees, attorneys, stakeholders and members of the public who will submit comments on ATF rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of standards and evaluative criteria from ATF's Proposed Rule revising the regulatory definition of "engaged in the business" as a dealer in firearms (27 CFR part 478), including interpretive definitions, evidentiary presumptions, administrative procedures, and public-participation instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: "Engaged in the business" (dealer)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A person who devotes time, attention, and labor to dealing in firearms as a regular course of trade or business to predominantly earn a profit through the repetitive purchase and resale of firearms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wording is the core regulatory definition ATF proposes to keep. The Department explains the core concept as "the intent to engage in a course of repeated buying and selling predominantly motivated by profit." Example provided: buying ten of the same handgun with predominant intent to resell for profit and then repetitively selling them constitutes being engaged in the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal collection exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The term does not include "a person who makes occasional sales, exchanges, or purchases of firearms to enhance a personal collection or for a hobby, or who sells all or part of the person's personal collection of firearms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrow statutory exception recognizes collectors and hobbyists who occasionally buy/sell; Congress intended the exception to treat occasional, noncommercial sales differently from repetitive, profit-motivated dealing. ATF warns against narrowly limiting what qualifies as a personal collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of "predominantly earn a profit"
rubrics_metrics.description: "The intent underlying the sale or disposition of firearms is predominantly one of obtaining pecuniary gain, as opposed to other intents, such as improving or liquidating a personal firearms collection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF explains BSCA changed the statutory focus from "livelihood and profit" to "predominantly earn a profit," meaning the key inquiry is pecuniary intent rather than whether the activity is someone's primary livelihood. The rule also states: "proof of profit, including the intent to profit, is not required in cases in which the person engaged in the regular and repetitive purchase and disposition of firearms for criminal purposes or terrorism."

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee personal collection—specific criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: For firearms imported, manufactured, or acquired by a licensee, the personal collection includes only firearms that were: (a) acquired/transferred without intent to willfully evade restrictions; (b) recorded by the licensee as an acquisition per §§ 478.122(a), 478.123(a), or 478.125(e) (unless acquired prior to licensure and not intended for sale); (c) recorded as a disposition from business inventory to personal collection per those same recordkeeping sections (unless acquired prior to licensure and not intended for sale); (d) maintained in the personal collection for at least one year from the date transferred; and (e) stored separately from business inventory and identified as "not for sale" when on business premises (e.g., by attaching a tag).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five subcriteria establish when a licensee's firearm counts as a personal-collection item rather than business inventory; they impose recordkeeping, holding-period, and storage/identification requirements to prevent commingling business inventory with a purported personal collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of fact-pattern presumptions (27 CFR 478.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: ATF proposes to remove and reserve § 478.13, eliminating the EIB rule's fact-pattern presumptions (e.g., presumptions triggered by repetitively reselling firearms within 30 days of purchase, or within one year if new or same make/model; or by engaging merchant services to repetitively accept payments for firearms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF's rationale: the presumptions risked improperly shifting the burden of proof, were unnecessary given the statutory standard, were not used in civil or criminal proceedings in practice, and could be perceived as relieving the Government of its burden. ATF states actions identified by those presumptions remain admissible circumstantial evidence but should not carry dispositive presumption status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary role of circumstantial facts vs legal presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts identified in prior regulatory presumptions may constitute circumstantial evidence from which a factfinder could conclude a person was engaged in the business, but those facts should not be elevated into mandatory or dispositive legal presumptions that shift the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF emphasizes that removing regulatory presumptions "simply prevents this evidence from being given dispositive effect unless the firearm seller can carry the burden of disproving that he was engaged in the business." Courts/juries may consider the facts but the Government must still meet its burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright-line numerical threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no "magic number of sales" that automatically makes a person engaged in the business; the statutory definition is a qualitative standard, not a fixed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF stresses fact-specific application: selling two firearms could constitute dealing if accompanied by labor and profit intent; selling fifty could still be a liquidating personal collection absent contrary facts. The rule draws on judicial precedent recognizing qualitative standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors courts consider in determining 'engaged in the business'
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of factors may be considered including: (1) the quantity and frequency of sales; (2) the location of the sales; (3) conditions under which the sales occurred; (4) the defendant's behavior before, during, and after the sales; (5) the price charged; (6) the characteristics of the firearms sold; and (7) the intent of the seller at the time of the sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF cites circuit decisions and pattern jury instructions (e.g., 5th and 9th Circuits) and notes judges already instruct jurors on such factors; these are the typical, nonexhaustive considerations in fact-specific inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different treatment across enforcement contexts (criminal, civil, administrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mandatory or legal presumptions cannot be employed in criminal proceedings (e.g., Sandstrom v. Montana), criminal prosecutions require willfulness mens rea under 18 U.S.C. 924(a)(1)(D), and ATF's administrative license revocation processes typically apply to already-licensed persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF explains that presumptions were not appropriate for criminal cases and that administrative enforcement (license revocation) and civil asset forfeiture have different evidentiary and procedural contexts; ATF notes it has not used the EIB presumptions in civil proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory goal test (what the EIB rule sought and why it failed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB rule stated objectives to (1) license more persons; (2) deter unlicensed dealing; (3) increase background checks by increasing licensed population; and (4) expand crime-gun trace requests by increasing licensees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF reports empirical review showing Type 01 (dealer) applications and total licensees declined since 2021 and did not increase after the EIB rule, supporting the agency's conclusion that the presumptions/rule failed to achieve intended outcomes and thus justifying repeal of the presumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuance of business — transfer and recordkeeping requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When discontinuing business, a former licensee must transfer former licensee inventory to a responsible person to whom receipt/possession/sale or disposition is not prohibited by law, and transfers to a licensee or responsible person "shall be appropriately recorded as dispositions" in accordance with §§ 478.122(b), 478.123(b), or 478.125(e) prior to delivering records after discontinuing business (amendments to §§ 478.57 and 478.78).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions govern how former licensee inventory must be handled and documented upon business discontinuance or operations after notice; ATF is retaining discontinuance-related provisions while removing other EIB provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-comment procedural requirements and guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must be submitted by the published deadline (must be submitted or postmarked on or before August 4, 2026); submissions must include the agency name and RIN (RIN 1140-AB01); acceptable submission methods: Regulations.gov e-rulemaking portal (follow instructions) or mail to specified ATF Rulemaking Comments address; comments not accepted via the listed email address; the federal e-rulemaking portal will not accept comments after midnight Eastern Time on the last day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All comments are considered public and may be posted without change; the agency may redact or withhold certain submissions or portions; instructions caution commenters who do not want PII posted to omit it from the body and attachments or place such information in a separate attachment and mark it (see next metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of personally identifying information and proprietary information in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If commenters do not want PII posted, they should omit it from the body of the comment and any uploaded attachments to be posted; if they wish to submit PII, they should place it in a separate attachment and mark it at the top with "CUI//PRVCY." Business proprietary information should be similarly placed in a separate attachment and marked "CUI//PROPIN." Mail submissions should likewise omit PII from the body and provide such information on the cover sheet only marked accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF will post properly completed comments to Regulations.gov; marking attachments as CUI is the agency's instructed procedure to indicate the desire for confidentiality, but commenters are warned that all comments are considered public and the agency may redact or withhold content at its discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for hearing and other public-participation options
rubrics_metrics.description: The document includes a "Request for Hearing" heading and invites public participation (comments sought, confidentiality, submitting comments, request for hearing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While detailed procedures for requesting a hearing are referenced under the "Public Participation" section, the page instructs interested parties on submitting written comments and refers readers to additional details in the SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION; commenters may also view alternative ways to comment and may use Regulations.gov docket (docket ATF-2026-0074).
